item.title: Javokhir Sindarov survives in first real fight of world title match
item.description: Third straight draw leaves title match at 1½–1½ Sindarov drops to eight seconds on move 39 Gukesh Dommaraju plays white after first rest day All your Gukesh v Sindarov questions, answered After two quieter draws, the world chess championship came to life on Thursday as Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov came within eight seconds of sudden death before fighting back to split the point with India’s Gukesh Dommaraju after nearly five hours. Their spirited 60-move battle at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs left their $2.5m match level at 1½–1½ heading into the first rest day. Gukesh, playing with the black pieces, returned to the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez, the opening he used in Tuesday’s 38-move opener . The defending champion sprang the first surprise on move five (5 … Be7), bringing out his bishop before retreating the knight that had taken Sindarov’s e-pawn, putting the challenger behind on time for the first time in the match. item.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
item.description: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. item.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
item.description: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

They were “the Bash Street Kids of punk”, in writer Jon Savage’s memorable estimation: “While other groups were carefully considering their moves,” he wrote, “the Damned went out there and pulled faces at the world as if there was no tomorrow.” Even their debut single New Rose implied they knew their time was limited: “I better go,” sang Dave Vanian amid its frantic thunder, “or it’ll be too late.” How wrong can you be? The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. item.title: Lumière album review – finding solace in the rich, lyrical world of French cello music
item.description: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasiona

item.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
item.description: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. item.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
item.description: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). item.title: ‘When I cut these women out I feel like I’m freeing them’: the feminist collage artists taking scissors to the patriarchy
item.description: A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto. The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. item.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power
item.description: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading.

I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. item.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
item.description: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. item.description: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. item.title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
item.description: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. item.title: The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon
item.description: Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes. It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! item.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
item.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. item.title: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
item.description: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak , which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating . Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason
item.description: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

item.title: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy
item.description: Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi . Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. item.title: ‘Nobody showed up but me’: will Friendsgiving survive gen Z?
item.description: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. item.title: The 4thWrite short story prize winner – a tale of teenage girlhood
item.description: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying o

item.title: Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election?
item.description: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro , an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation. “Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.” Continue reading...

item.title: Steal a chopper listening to Liszt! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical
item.description: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprises of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. item.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
item.description: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

item.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
item.description: The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered. Continue reading...

item.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
item.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously,

item.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
item.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it.

item.description: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. item.title: A moment that changed me: at 31 I felt I was running out of time – then my 83-year-old grandma got a tattoo
item.description: With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong … It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back o

item.title: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0 Awe, anxiety and opportunity: mathematics community shares mixed emotions following the solution of the field’s biggest unsolved problem.

item.title: Just eight universities dominate Nobel and other top economics prizes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03333-3 Economics is the outlier — top prizes in science, engineering and other social sciences go to researchers at a greater variety of institutions.

item.title: An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 Reconstruction of radiative forcing resulting from worldwide peatland drainage over the past two centuries reveals a persistent net warming effect caused by the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions over that of avoided CH4 emissions.

item.title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11275-z A multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human coronary artery disease provides a framework for mapping disease-associated genetic variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

item.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 Architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer drive cell state diversification through mechanochemical reprogramming of stem cell identities.

item.title: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

item.title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11353-2 Quantum confocal microscopy enables deterministic preparation of high-photon-number Fock-like states with up to 500 photons, reducing photon-number variance by 21.5 dB and achieving record displacement-sensing precision 19.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit.

item.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11287-9 RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) is enhanced by redesigned TnsA and a holo complex whose coordinated conformational licensing reveals a conserved mechanistic framework for engineering highly active CASTs.

item.title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11341-6 Dental morphology and proteomic analyses of fossils from southern China identify lineages with and without Denisovan affinity, indicating the diversity of hominin populations in this region in the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

item.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5 Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.

item.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11146-7 Integrated photonics could overcome key size, power and performance trade-offs in augmented-reality glasses, enabling compact, efficient displays while opening opportunities across quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

item.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11309-6 Coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas are demonstrated in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains, providing a foundation for topologically protected qubits in longer chains.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11196-x Structural analyses reveal the mechanism underlying RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) and provide a framework for developing CASTs into site-specific genome-editing tools.

item.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11231-x This Review covers the current state of research into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) from a variety of perspectives, focusing on the clinical context.

item.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11151-w The use of an extremophile fungus-derived gene decouples the trade-off of drought stress and reduced crop yield by boosting drought resilience and increasing yields in wheat, rice and maize.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

item.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

item.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

item.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

item.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

item.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
item.description: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

item.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

item.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
item.description: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

item.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
item.description: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

item.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
item.description: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
item.description: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

item.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
item.description: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

item.description: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

item.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
